title: From Homeless in Manhattan to Cooking for Its Mayor: Vikas Khanna's Extraordinary Full Circle
excerpt: The Michelin-starred chef who once slept on New York's streets hosted Mayor Zohran Mamdani for Iftar at his restaurant Bungalow — a reunion 25 years in the making.
body:
In 2001, Vikas Khanna was broke, recently homeless, and starting over at a Tribeca restaurant called Salaam Bombay. He had survived what he describes as an abusive job and months without a fixed address in one of the world's most expensive cities. He was an unknown immigrant cook from Amritsar with outsized ambitions and very little else.

One evening, filmmaker Mira Nair walked into Salaam Bombay with her eight-year-old son, Zohran. Khanna cooked for them. They became acquaintances. Life moved on.

Twenty-five years later, that eight-year-old boy is the Mayor of New York City. And Vikas Khanna — now a Michelin-starred chef, bestselling author, documentary filmmaker, and the face of Indian cuisine in America — personally prepared an Iftar meal for him at Bungalow, his restaurant in Manhattan's East Village.

"No words to express my feelings today," Khanna wrote on Instagram. "And today, 25-plus years later, I had the honour of cooking for that same young boy — now a global leader shaping the future of New York City. Life truly comes full circle."

## The Table of Grace

Bungalow, which earned a Michelin Bib Gourmand within its first year of operation, was not decorated any differently for Mamdani's visit than it would be for any evening service. But the restaurant had set up what Khanna called a "Table of Grace" — a dedicated space holding items of faith and cultural significance: Islamic prayer beads, henna cones, Muslim prayer caps, ittar bottles, and surma containers, arranged alongside fresh flowers, candles, and incense.

Mamdani, who became New York's first Muslim mayor and the youngest to hold the office, broke his fast in the traditional manner — first with a date, then a full Iftar meal that Khanna had prepared with dishes from their Salaam Bombay days.

The evening was widely covered by Indian media, but it resonated especially with the diaspora. Here was an Indian immigrant chef hosting the son of one of India's most celebrated filmmakers — now the mayor of the most powerful city on earth — for a meal that bridged Hindu and Muslim traditions, Amritsar and Tribeca, homelessness and the highest corridors of power.

## A Restaurant Built on Grief and Gratitude

Bungalow itself carries an emotional story. Khanna opened the restaurant in March 2024 as a tribute to his late sister Radhika, who died in February 2022 from lupus, an autoimmune disease. The opening date — March 23 — was chosen because it would have been Radhika's 50th birthday.

"Bungalow is my last restaurant where I'm cooking 16 to 18 hours a day," Khanna has said. "It was my sister's dream, this was not even my dream."

The name evokes the sprawling family home — the bungalow — that anchors Indian domestic life, a space where food and family are inseparable. Khanna has described it as a tribute not just to Radhika but to "millions of kitchens, chefs, cookbook writers, street vendors, and home cooks across India — and most importantly to our mothers who have nurtured our souls forever."

## From Amritsar to Harvard

Khanna's trajectory reads like fiction but is meticulously documented. Born in Amritsar, he grew up cooking in his family's modest kitchen and trained at some of India's hospitality schools before immigrating to the United States. His early years in New York were brutal — a period he rarely discusses in detail except to acknowledge the homelessness and the exploitative jobs that preceded his breakthrough.

The breakthrough, when it came, was decisive. Khanna's first Michelin star — at Junoon — made him one of the few Indian chefs in the world to earn the distinction. His restaurant Kinara in Dubai, his role as a judge on Celebrity MasterChef India, and his documentary The Last Color have made him arguably the most recognisable Indian chef on the planet.

Harvard University's South Asian Association honoured him as its Person of the Year — a recognition that Khanna framed not as a personal achievement but as a milestone for Indian cuisine itself. "What a milestone for Indian cuisine! To be named Person of the Year by Harvard University's SAA is beyond words," he said. "This recognition is not just an award — it's a promise. A commitment to continue honouring our culture through every dish, every detail."

## What Khanna Means for the Diaspora

The Indian food world is full of success stories, but Khanna's carries a specific weight for NRIs. He did not come from culinary royalty or a well-funded restaurant group. He did not apprentice in Paris. He arrived as a working-class immigrant, hit bottom, and cooked his way up — using Indian flavours, Indian techniques, and an unapologetically Indian identity.

His insistence on staying in New York rather than opening in India is deliberate. "Nobody can deny the power of New York City," he has said. "I feel that it uplifts the cuisine and turns it into not just your economy, it increases the currency of the cuisine."

For a generation of Indian Americans navigating their own identity questions — how much to assimilate, how much to preserve, what to carry forward — Khanna offers a model that says you can be fully Indian and fully American and fully excellent, and that food is the bridge between all three.

The Iftar at Bungalow was just a dinner. But the story it tells — of an immigrant, a filmmaker's son, a prayer, a meal, and a city that made room for all of it — is the kind of story the diaspora does not hear often enough.
